planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or set out container plants in spring once soil is workable, in lean, gritty, very sharply drained soil; the thick white felt covering the leaves rots quickly in humid or poorly drained sites, so raised beds or slopes are ideal.

directions: Plant in lean, alkaline, fast-draining soil in full sun; woolly lavender is instantly recognizable by its dense, white, felt-like wool coating narrow leaves, a thicker covering than any other common lavender species. Deep violet-blue flower spikes rise above the silvery foliage in summer on a compact, rounded mound. It is native to limestone slopes in the Sierra Nevada of southern Spain and is markedly more sensitive to winter wet than English lavender, so skip mulch against the crown and avoid irrigation in winter. Because the wool traps moisture, good air circulation and strict avoidance of overhead watering are essential to prevent crown rot.

planting.note: Take tip cuttings or move container plants outdoors after all frost danger has passed, into well-drained potting mix or garden soil in full sun; this species is reliably damaged by frost and is usually grown as a container or patio plant outside zones 9-11.

directions: Grow in free-draining soil or a mineral-rich potting mix in full sun; jagged lavender is named for its soft, finely pinnately divided, silvery-gray leaves that give the plant a lacy, fern-like texture distinct from the toothed foliage of French lavender. Slender, nearly leafless stems carry small blue-violet flower spikes almost continuously in mild, frost-free climates, and the foliage carries only a faint, mild lavender scent rather than the strong aromatic oils of English or lavandin types. Native to the Canary Islands and Madeira, it is one of the more tender lavenders and should be brought under cover or grown as a seasonal container plant wherever winter temperatures regularly drop below the high 20s Fahrenheit. Light, frequent grooming of spent flower stems keeps the airy habit tidy and encourages continued bloom.

planting.note: Root cuttings or plant container stock in spring in lean, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; this species needs the same scrupulous drainage as other Mediterranean lavenders and resents heavy, wet winter soils.

directions: Plant in gritty, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; green lavender is the only widely grown lavender species with greenish-yellow flowers and bracts rather than blue or purple, making it an unusual accent among typical lavender plantings. Crushed foliage releases a sharp, pine-resin-like aroma that is noticeably different from the sweeter scent of English lavender. Native to Madeira, the Azores, and southwestern Iberia, it blooms over a long stretch from late spring into summer and benefits from a light shearing immediately after the main flush to maintain a dense, rounded form. It is somewhat less reliably perennial in humid summer climates than in dry Mediterranean-type gardens, so excellent air movement and drainage are key to longevity.

planting.note: Propagate by cuttings, since this species does not come reliably true from seed, and set out or move containers outdoors only after nighttime temperatures stay above the high 20s Fahrenheit; it thrives in Mediterranean and coastal climates but needs winter protection or indoor overwintering elsewhere.

directions: Grow in full sun in lean, fast-draining soil; Canary Island lavender is a large, fast-growing subshrub with deeply dissected, fern-like dark green leaves carried on reddish stems, giving it a distinctly shrubby, almost tree-like presence compared to compact English lavender. It produces slender purple-violet flower spikes nearly year-round in mild, frost-free gardens, though the foliage has a resinous, sage-like scent rather than the classic sweet lavender fragrance. Native to the Canary Islands, it is one of the most cold-tender species in the genus and is commonly grown in containers or conservatories in climates colder than zone 9, brought outdoors for summer and moved under cover before frost. Prune lightly after flowering flushes to control its vigorous size and maintain a bushy shape.

planting.note: This sterile hybrid must be propagated by cuttings and does not come true from seed; plant container stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun once the soil is workable.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, giving this vigorous hybrid plenty of room; Allard's lavender is a naturally occurring cross between French lavender (Lavandula dentata) and spike lavender (Lavandula latifolia) that combines the large, toothed, gray-green leaves of dentata with the bigger stature and camphor-tinged scent inherited from latifolia. Pale lavender-blue flower spikes are carried on long stems well above the foliage and appear almost continuously in mild climates, making it one of the showiest and longest-blooming lavenders for frost-free gardens. It is more cold-tender than either English lavender or straight French lavender, so in regions colder than zone 8 it is best grown in a large container and moved indoors or into a greenhouse for winter. Cut back hard after the main bloom flush to control its naturally large, sprawling size.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or set out container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; this silvery form is slightly more cold-sensitive than typical French lavender, so wait until frost danger has fully passed in marginal zones.

directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; candicans lavender is a densely white-hairy, silver-leaved form of French lavender whose toothed, felted foliage glows noticeably brighter than the gray-green leaves of typical Lavandula dentata. It carries the same oblong, pale-purple, feathery-bracted flower spikes and strong aromatic scent as standard French lavender, often in slightly larger, showier spikes, and blooms nearly year-round in mild climates. It shares French lavender's intolerance of heavy or constantly damp soils and benefits from the same light post-bloom trimming to prevent legginess. Its brighter silver foliage makes it a particularly effective textural contrast plant in drought-tolerant borders and herb gardens.
